The words

God of the changing year, whose arm of power
In safety leads through danger's darkest hour, —
Here in Thy temple bow Thy children down,
To bless Thy mercy, and Thy might to own.

Thine are the beams that cheer us on our way,
And pour around the gladdening light of day;
Thine is the night, and the fair orbs that shine
To cheer its hours of darkness, — all are Thine.

If round our path the thorns of sorrow grew,
And mortal friends were faithless, Thou wast true
Did sickness shake the frame, or anguish tear
The wounded spirit, Thou wast present there.

O, lend Thine ear, and lift our voice to Thee;
Where'er we dwell, still let Thy mercy be;
From year to year, still nearer to Thy shrine
Draw our frail hearts, and make them wholly Thine!

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum F and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on s (C).
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Emily Taylor wrote these words. They were printed in A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion, compiled by Samuel Longfellow and Samuel Johnson (Boston, 1848), as hymn 400, “The Changing Year”.

The book printed the words without tunes, marked Tens (10.10.10.10), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to SONG TWENTY-TWO; any other Tens tune fits them as well.

  • Words: Emily Taylor (1795–1872)
  • Music (1623): Orlando Gibbons (1583–1625)

Tune SONG TWENTY-TWO by Orlando Gibbons (1583–1625); words by Emily Taylor (1795–1872).

Sung to the same tune: Breathe Thoughts of Pity O'er a Brother's Fall, Cheer Up, My Soul, There Is a Mercy-seat, Father! There Is No Change to Live with Thee, Though Lonely Be Thy Path, Fear Not, for He.

Questions about God of the Changing Year, Whose Arm of Power

What is the doh of God of the Changing Year, Whose Arm of Power?

In this version, in F major, doh is F. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does God of the Changing Year, Whose Arm of Power start on?

It starts on s (C in F major). Find doh first, then sing up or down to s.

Is God of the Changing Year, Whose Arm of Power in the public domain?

Yes. Emily Taylor died in 1872, Orlando Gibbons died in 1625; the words were in print by 1848 and the music in 1623. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
